name: Keloid surgery + radiation
lead: Keloid excision with adjuvant radiation therapy is a combination in which a raised, overgrown scar is surgically removed and the wound is then treated with radiation to reduce regrowth. For people with keloids on visible sites such as the earlobes, chest, shoulders or jawline, the aim is a flatter, less conspicuous scar that stays that way. Wikipedia reports that excision alone has a recurrence rate of 70 to 100 percent, that recurrences can be larger, and that adding radiation, pressure therapy or laser sharply lowers recurrence; it adds that radiation is not recommended for children because of growth-abnormality risk [1].

Published studies describe surgery plus radiotherapy as a standard approach for severe keloids; one 2020 paper states that radiotherapy is essential for preventing recurrence [2]. A 2026 systematic review of 22 studies and more than 2,219 patients reported recurrence after excision and postoperative radiotherapy ranging from 1.6 to 55.2 percent depending on dose, fractionation, technique and follow-up [16]. Researchers also study adjuncts: hyperbaric oxygen, steroid injection, botulinum toxin, photobiomodulation and tension-reducing suturing [3][4][5][6][7].

Keloids most often affect people of sub-Saharan African, Asian or Latin American ancestry and commonly follow earlobe piercing [1]. Because the treatment is delivered by clinicians in surgical and radiation-oncology settings, it appears in looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion mainly as the medical route for scars from piercings, acne and surgery rather than as a do-it-yourself practice.

paras: A keloid is a benign scar in which collagen overgrows beyond the original wound edge. It is not contagious, but it can itch, hurt, change skin texture and, in severe cases, limit movement of the skin [1]. Almost any skin injury can trigger one, including burns, acne, chickenpox scars, ear piercings, surgical incisions and vaccination sites, and keloids sometimes arise with no obvious injury [1].

Wikipedia distinguishes keloids from hypertrophic scars, which also contain excess collagen but stay within the boundary of the original wound and often flatten over one to two years [20]. Keloids are more likely at high-tension sites, and a 2026 review reports they occur up to 15 times more often in people with darker skin pigmentation [16].

Excision removes the keloid tissue; adjuvant radiation, delivered as electron-beam, superficial or brachytherapy treatment, targets the wound bed afterwards. A 2023 study examined risk factors for recurrence after keloid surgery with electron radiotherapy [8], and a registered study followed high dose rate brachytherapy in 43 patients [9].

Reported radiotherapy schedules vary widely across studies. A 2026 review noted the absence of standardized guidelines for dose, fractionation and timing, and that most adverse effects were mild to moderate and limited to the treated area; the authors could not establish a direct causal link between postoperative radiotherapy and secondary malignancy [16].

A 2020 report with geometric modelling and a retrospective cohort assessed superficial and deep fascia tensile reduction in severe keloid surgery, proposing that reduced skin tension helps outcomes [2]. A 1998 paper described reconstructing the earlobe with a subcutaneous island pedicle flap after earlobe keloid resection, noting that large earlobe keloids are hard to treat by non-surgical means [10].

A 2018 randomized study of 240 patients examined hyperbaric oxygen therapy after excision and radiotherapy for reducing recurrence [3]. A randomized trial studied immediate triamcinolone injection after auricular keloid surgery [4], and a 1994 report described steroid injection after surgery [11]. Botulinum toxin combined with superficial radiotherapy after chest keloid surgery was analysed in a 2025 paper [5], and a 2022 trial protocol proposed photobiomodulation with steroid injection around surgery, noting that no gold-standard treatment exists [6]. Registered trials include excision with steroid injection after caesarean (146 participants) [12], imiquimod (terminated) [13] and siRNA microneedle patches [14].

sections.h: Research on dose, site and children
paras: A 2026 meta-regression by Lin and colleagues analysed 94 patient cohorts covering 9,909 lesions from 57 studies. It found that anatomical location, a proxy for skin tension, was the only significant predictor of recurrence: low-tension sites had a 70.5 percent lower recurrence risk than high-tension sites, and biologically effective dose was not significant after adjusting for site. The authors recommended site-specific, tension-based guidelines [17].

Radiation in children is traditionally avoided because of concern about radiation-induced malignancy and growth effects [1]. A 2026 case series and systematic review in Annals of Plastic Surgery, from Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and published studies, pooled 60 patients with 85 recurrent keloids (mean age 14.4 years, earlobes the most common site at 38.3 percent). Overall recurrence was 22.4 percent, hyperpigmentation 53.3 percent and transient itching 15 percent, with no secondary malignancies or growth disturbances over a mean follow-up of about 32 months; the authors called for long-term prospective studies [18].

The trials and cohorts above are mostly small, retrospective or protocol-stage. Systematic reviews describe wide recurrence ranges for excision plus radiotherapy, from 1.6 to 55.2 percent in one review of 22 studies, and note that differences in dose, technique, site and follow-up make direct comparison difficult [16][19]. A 2018 randomized study of 240 patients examined hyperbaric oxygen after excision and radiotherapy [3], and registered trials include a high-dose-rate brachytherapy study in 43 patients starting in 2003 [9]. A large registered retrospective study of keloid disorder planned 5,000 participants [15].

Keloids come up in appearance discussions mainly around piercings, acne scarring and surgical scars, and the treatment is a clinician-delivered medical procedure rather than a home practice. Community claims about this combination are not documented here.

Wikipedia lists ancestry from sub-Saharan Africa, Asia or Latin America, darker skin tone, family history and age between roughly 10 and 30 as risk factors; about one-third of people with keloids have an affected first-degree relative, and susceptibility loci have been reported on chromosome 15 although no single causative gene is known [1]. Reported prevalence estimates range widely, from 4.5 to 16 percent in some populations, and a 2001 review cited incidence from 16 percent in the Democratic Republic of the Congo to 0.09 percent in England [1]. Survivors of the 1945 atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki are cited as an example of large keloids following extensive thermal or radiation burns [1].

Common sites are the earlobes, arms, pelvic region, collarbone area, central chest after sternotomy, and the back and shoulders after acne [1]. Wikipedia advises avoiding unnecessary trauma such as elective ear piercing in people prone to keloids; this is stated as general medical guidance in that source [1].

Excision is the most common surgical option but, used alone, is reported to recur in 70 to 100 percent of cases, sometimes larger than the original [1]. Alongside radiation, Wikipedia describes intralesional triamcinolone injections (introduced in the mid-1960s), cryotherapy, pressure therapy used since the 1970s, silicone gel sheeting introduced in the early 1980s, and a triple therapy for adults combining corticosteroids, 5-fluorouracil and pulsed dye laser [1]. A 2022 Cochrane review is cited as finding too little evidence to say whether silicone gel sheeting or laser outperforms other options [1].

A 2026 systematic review by Wojarska and colleagues covered 21 studies and more than 8,627 patients and reported recurrence ranges for adjuncts after excision: postoperative brachytherapy 3.1 to 15 percent, external-beam radiotherapy 14 to 29.3 percent, compression 10.66 and 14 percent (particularly for ear keloids), and triamcinolone injection 6.6 to 33 percent depending on protocol. Imiquimod gave higher and less consistent recurrence, and combination therapies outperformed single treatments. No meta-analysis was done because protocols varied too widely [19].

timeline.event: Intralesional triamcinolone injection is introduced for keloids (mid-1960s). [1]
Pressure therapy begins to be used for keloids. [1]
A report describes intralesional steroid injection following keloid surgery. [11]
A subcutaneous island pedicle flap is described for earlobe reconstruction after keloid resection. [10]
A registered high-dose-rate brachytherapy study for keloids begins, later enrolling 43 patients. [9]
A randomized study of hyperbaric oxygen after keloid surgery and radiotherapy is published. [3]
A paper on fascial tension reduction in severe keloid surgery states that radiotherapy is essential for preventing recurrence. [2]
A Cochrane review is cited as finding insufficient evidence on silicone gel sheeting and laser. [1]
Systematic reviews, a meta-regression of 9,909 lesions and a pediatric case series report on adjuvant radiotherapy. [16][17][18][19]

card.summary: Cutting out a keloid and radiating the wound bed, a clinical standard for severe cases with many add-on studies.
card.note: Surgical alone recurrence is reported at 70 to 100 percent; radiation is not recommended for children per Wikipedia.

quick.overview:
The keloid is surgically removed and the area is treated with radiation to lower regrowth. Wikipedia reports very high recurrence after excision alone and lower recurrence with radiation or other adjuncts.

Studies examine add-ons such as steroid injection, hyperbaric oxygen and botulinum toxin.
quick.mechanism: Surgery removes the scar tissue; radiation is used to suppress renewed fibroblast growth in the wound.
quick.risks: Recurrence, sometimes larger, is the main documented problem; radiation is not recommended in children for growth reasons per Wikipedia.

chain: Radiation to the wound bed suppresses renewed scar-forming cell activity
A flatter scar that is less likely to regrow larger than the original
angle.text: Clinicians use excision with radiation to remove a raised keloid and lower the chance it returns, so that a visible site such as an earlobe or chest stays flatter. The reported recurrence range varies widely across studies and sites.
